items.question: A company issues debentures without giving any undertaking to repay the money borrowed during its lifetime; they are repayable only on the winding up of the company or after a very long period. Such debentures are called:
items.proposed_explanation: Irredeemable (perpetual) debentures carry no undertaking for repayment of the money borrowed and are repayable on winding up or after a long period. Redeemable debentures are payable on the expiry of a specific period, convertible debentures can be converted into shares or other securities, and secured debentures are those on which a charge is created on the company's assets.

Current Liabilities
The quick assets are defined as those assets which are quickly convertible
into cash. While calculating quick assets we exclude the inventories at the end
and other current assets such as prepaid expenses, advance tax, etc., from the
current assets. Because of exclusion of non-liquid current assets it is considered
better than current ratio as a measure of liquidity position of the business. It is
calculated to serve as a supplementary check on liquidity position of the business
and is therefore, also known as ‘Acid-Test Ratio’.

items.question: Which of the following is a capital receipt of the government?

options.text: Proceeds from the sale of its shares in public sector undertakings

items.proposed_explanation: Capital receipts are receipts that either create a liability or reduce the government's financial assets. Selling shares in PSUs (disinvestment) reduces its financial assets, so it is a capital receipt. Taxes collected and dividends received neither create a liability nor reduce the government's financial assets, so they are not capital receipts.

According to NCERT Macroeconomics (Chapter 5: Government Budget and the Economy), capital receipts are those receipts that either create a liability or cause a reduction in the assets of the government. The proceeds from the sale of shares in Public Sector Undertakings (disinvestment) reduce the financial assets of the government, making them capital receipts (specifically non-debt creating capital receipts). Goods and services tax (B) and income tax (D) are tax revenue receipts, while dividends from PSUs (C) are non-tax revenue receipts, as none of them create liabilities or reduce government assets.

items.question: In an economy with a single bank, the bank must keep 20 per cent of its deposits as cash reserves. It starts with a fresh cash deposit of ₹100, and every loan it gives comes back to it as a deposit. What is the maximum total amount of deposits the bank can have?
items.proposed_explanation: Lending continues until the required reserves equal the ₹100 of cash the bank holds. Required reserves are 20 per cent of deposits, so 0.20 × Total deposits = ₹100 and Total deposits = ₹500 (a money multiplier of 1/0.20 = 5). ₹180 is only the total after the first loan of ₹80 returns as a deposit, ₹120 simply adds 20 to the first deposit, and ₹2,000 wrongly multiplies ₹100 by 20.

independently_solved_keys.derivation: With a 20% reserve ratio, maximum deposits are the initial cash reserve divided by the reserve ratio: ₹100 ÷ 0.20 = ₹500. The supplied NCERT excerpt also describes this one-bank example and states that deposits reach ₹500 when required reserves reach ₹100.

The maximum total deposits generated by an initial cash deposit is determined by the deposit multiplier formula: Total Deposits = Initial Deposit / Reserve Ratio. With an initial cash deposit of ₹100 and a cash reserve ratio of 20% (0.20), the deposit multiplier is 1 / 0.20 = 5. Therefore, the maximum total deposits the bank can hold are 100 × 5 = ₹500, at which point all ₹100 of original cash serves as required reserves.

Apart from the CRR, banks are also required to keep some reserves
in liquid form in the short term. This ratio is called Statutory Liquidity
Ratio or SLR.
In our fictional example, suppose CRR = 20 per cent, then with deposits of Rs
100, our bank will need to keep Rs 20 (20 per cent of 100) as cash reserves. Only
the remaining amount of deposits, i.e., Rs 80 (100 – 20 = 80) can be used to give
loans. The statutory requirement of the reserve ratio acts as a limit to the amount
of credit that banks can create.
We can understand this by going back to our fictional example of an economy
with one bank. Let us assume that our bank starts with a deposit of Rs 100
made by Leela. The reserve ratio is 20 per cent. Thus our bank has Rs 80 (100 – 20)

bank’s deposits in the next round as liabilities, making a total of Rs 180 as

reserves. Recall that our bank had started with Rs 100 as cash. Since it is
required to keep only Rs 36 as reserves, it can lend Rs 64 again (100 – 36 = 64).
The bank lends out Rs 64 to Junaid. This in turn shows up in the bank as
deposits. The process keeps repeating itself till all the required reserves become

items.question: A company's current assets are ₹1,20,000. Its only current liabilities are trade payables of ₹60,000 and a bank overdraft. What is its current ratio?
items.proposed_explanation: Current ratio = Current assets : Current liabilities = ₹1,20,000 : ₹60,000 = 2 : 1.

Current liabilities include trade payables and short-term borrowings such as a bank overdraft (E2.1, E3.1), so current liabilities = ₹60,000 + x. A ratio of 3:1 would require liabilities of ₹40,000, less than the stated trade payables alone. A ratio of 2:1 would require total liabilities of ₹60,000, leaving no balance for the stated overdraft.
